Chapter 20 — Special Considerations in Treatment for Adults

▸ In the 7th edition this is Chapter 20 (two new clear-aligner chapters shifted the tail) — figure references keep their 6th-edition numbers.

Plain text is your original summary, kept word-for-word. Coloured boxes are genuine 7th-edition additions/revisions (compared against the 7th's Ch 20); red marks important cautions. (This chapter has no cropped figures yet, so figure references appear as text only.)
Adjunctive Versus Comprehensive Treatment
  • In general, orthodontists consider adults as those whose growth is essentially completed. The mean cutoff age for females is 18, but for males it is 20 or 21.
  • Adjunctive orthodontic treatment for adults is, by definition, tooth movement carried out to facilitate other dental procedures necessary to control disease, restore function, and/or enhance appearance.
  • Comprehensive orthodontics for adults tends to be difficult and technically demanding.
Principles of Adjunctive Treatment

I Treatment Goals

  • Whatever the occlusal status originally, the goals of adjunctive treatment should be to:
    • Improve periodontal health by eliminating plaque-harboring areas and improving alveolar ridge contour
    • Establish favorable crown-root ratios and position the teeth so that occlusal forces are transmitted along the long axes of the teeth
    • Facilitate restorative treatment: More ideal and conservative techniques and optimal esthetics.
  • Typically, adjunctive orthodontic treatment will involve any or all of several procedures:
    1. Repositioning teeth after extractions or bone loss so that implants can be placed or more ideal fixed or removable partial dentures can be fabricated.
    2. Aligning anterior teeth to allow more esthetic restorations or successful splinting
    3. Correcting crossbite if this compromises jaw function (not all crossbites do)
    4. Forcing eruption of badly broken-down teeth either to: expose sound root structure on which to place crowns, or level bone margins and regenerate alveolar bone
  • Orthodontic treatment for (TMD) should not be considered adjunctive treatment.
  • Intrusion: a general guideline in treatment of adults with periodontal involvement and bone loss, lower incisor teeth that are excessively extruded are best treated by reduction of crown height. (crown-to-root ratio)
  • Crowding of more that 3 to 4 mm should not be attempted by stripping enamel from the contact surfaces of the anterior teeth. It may be advantageous to strip posterior teeth to provide space for alignment of the incisors, but this requires a complete orthodontic appliance and cannot be considered adjunctive treatment.

II Diagnostic and Treatment Planning Considerations

  • In adjunctive treatment, the restorative dentist usually is the principal architect of the treatment plan
  • For dentally compromised population, the records usually should include individual intraoral radiographs to supplement the panoramic radiograph
  • For adjunctive orthodontics with a partial fixed appliance, pretreatment cephalometric radiographs usually are not required
  • With efficient use of orthodontic appliances, it should be possible to reach the objectives of adjunctive treatment within 6 months.

III Biomechanical Considerations

Characteristics of the Orthodontic Appliance

  • When a partial fixed appliance is to be used for adjunctive treatment, with the possible exception of alignment of anterior teeth, the 22-slot edgewise appliance with twin brackets is preferred. (allows the use of stiffer stabilizing wires). (use wires smaller than bracket to reduce torque)
  • Removable appliances of the traditional plastic-and-wire type are rarely satisfactory for adjunctive treatment.
  • In a partial fixed appliance for adjunctive treatment, the brackets are placed in an ideal position only on teeth to be moved, and the remaining teeth in the anchor system to be engaged passively Fig 19.2.
Generalized (7th) The 7th no longer hard-specifies the 22-slot — it says "an edgewise appliance with biomechanical characteristics like those of twin brackets is preferred," and makes the larger slot conditional ("if a larger slot size is used…").

Effects of Reduced Periodontal Support

  • When bone is lost, the PDL area decrease, and the same force against the crown produces greater pressure in the PDL of the periodontally compromised tooth than a normally supported one.
  • The greater the loss of attachment, the smaller the area of supported root and the further apical the center of resistance will become Fig 19.3. In general terms, tooth movement is quite possible despite bone loss, but lighter forces and relatively larger moments are needed.
New detail (7th) The 7th quantifies this: for a tooth whose center of resistance is now 15 mm apical to the bracket, a 100-g force produces a 1500 g-mm moment on a smaller PDL area — roughly twice the optimal pressure — and the moment is not large enough to prevent tipping.

IV Timing and Sequence of Treatment Fig 19.4

  • Restorations requiring detailed occlusal anatomy should not be placed until any adjunctive orthodontic treatment has been completed because the occlusion inevitably will be changed.
  • Surgical pocket elimination and osseous surgical procedures (not disease control) should be delayed until completion of the orthodontic phase of treatment because significant soft tissue and bony recontouring occurs during orthodontic tooth movement.
Adjunctive Treatment Procedures

I Uprighting Posterior Teeth

Treatment Planning Considerations

  • Should both the second and third molars be uprighted? If the third molar would move it into a position in which good hygiene could not be maintained or it would not be in functional occlusion. In these circumstances, it is more appropriate to extract the third molar and simply upright the second molar tooth.
  • How should the tipped teeth be uprighted? By distal crown movement (tipping) "open space", or by mesial root movement "reduce or even close the space"? If extensive ridge resorption has already occurred, particularly in the buccolingual dimension, closing the space by mesial movement of a wide molar root into the narrow alveolar ridge will proceed very slowly. (the treatment time can be as much as 3 years)
  • Uprighting a mesially tipped tooth by tipping it distally also extrudes it. Fig 19.7
  • Uprighting one second molar by distal crown tipping, the simplest cases should be completed in 8 to 10 weeks, but uprighting two molars in the same quadrant could easily take 6 months.

Appliances for Molar Uprighting — Distal Crown Tipping

  • A partial fixed appliance (bonded brackets on the premolars and canine in that quadrant)
  • A general guideline is that molar bands are best when the periodontal condition allows. The greater the degree of periodontal breakdown around the molar, the more a bonded attachment should be considered.
  • If the molar is only moderately tipped, treatment often can be accomplished with a flexible rectangular wire. The best choice is 17 × 25 austenitic nickel‒titanium (A-NiTi) that delivers approximately 100 gm of force. With this material, a single wire may complete the necessary uprighting. Fig 19.8
  • It is important to relieve the occlusion as the tooth tips upright. Failure to do this may cause excessive tooth mobility and increase treatment time.
  • If the molar is severely tipped, a continuous wire that uprights the molar will have side effects on the position and inclination of the second premolar. For that reason it is better to carry out the bulk of the uprighting by using an auxiliary uprighting spring Fig 19.9.
  • Distal tipping of a single molar on both sides can be done at the same time, but then a bonded lingual stabilizing wire canine-to-canine should be placed to control the incisor position.

Mesial Root Movement

  • Skeletal anchorage is required if the goal is to close the old extraction space.
  • If a small amount of mesial movement to prevent opening too much space is the goal (with distal crown tipping), a single T-loop sectional archwire of 17 × 25 stainless steel or 19 × 25 beta-Ti wire can be effective Fig 19.10.
  • Opening the T-loop by 1 to 2 mm, and then bent sharply gingivally to maintain this opening. This activation provides a mesial force on the molar that counteracts distal crown tipping while the tooth uprights.
  • The T-loop appliance also is indicated if the molar to be uprighted is severely tipped but has no occlusal antagonist (T-loop minimizes the extrusion that accompanies uprighting, which can be excessive with the other methods when there is no antagonist).

Final Positioning of Molar and Premolars

  • Once molar uprighting is almost complete, often it is desirable to increase the available pontic space and close open contacts in the anterior segment. Fig 19.11

Uprighting Two Molars in the Same Quadrant

  • The goal should be a modest amount of distal crown tipping of both teeth, which typically would leave space for a premolar-sized implant or pontic.
  • In the lower arch, a bonded canine-to-canine lingual stabilizing wire (which is similar to a bonded retainer) is needed to control the position of anterior teeth
  • Trying to upright both the second and third molars bilaterally at the same time is not a good idea; significant movement of the anchor teeth is inevitable unless skeletal anchorage is used.
  • Third molar should carry a single rectangular tube and the second molar a bracket. (increase flexibility-span)
  • Use a highly flexible wire initially‒17 × 25 A-NiTi then proceed to a TMA wire of the same size.

Retention

  • If bone grafting and implant surgery is planned or restoration is delayed, "A-splint" is preferred Fig 19.12

II Crossbite Correction

  • Posterior crossbites frequently are corrected using "through the bite" elastics (cross-elastics). (tends to extrude teeth, should be used only for a short time). Fig 19.13
  • Often it is desirable to move the maxillary teeth more than the mandibular. One way to do that is to have several teeth in the lower arch stabilized by a heavy archwire segment (could be used in reverse)
  • If an anterior crossbite is due only to a displaced tooth and correcting it requires only tipping, then a removable appliance or clear aligner may be used "this also produce an apparent intrusion Fig 19.14"

III Extrusion

Treatment Planning

  • Controlled extrusion (sometimes called forced eruption) can be an excellent alternative to extensive crown-lengthening surgery.
  • Its advantages over crown-lengthening surgery:
    • Can allow isolation under a rubber dam for endodontic therapy when it would not be possible otherwise
    • It allows crown margins to be placed on sound tooth structure while maintaining a uniform gingival contour
    • The alveolar bone height is not compromised, the apparent crown length is maintained, and the bony support of adjacent teeth is not compromised.
  • For some patients, the orthodontic movement must be completed before definitive endodontic procedures to provide better access for endodontic and restorative procedures. If so, preliminary endodontic treatment to relieve symptoms is done initially, and the tooth is maintained with a temporary root filling or other palliative treatment until it has been moved to a better position.
  • The distance the tooth should be extruded is determined by three things:
    1. The location of the defect (e.g., fracture line, root perforation, or resorption site)
    2. Space to place the margin of the restoration so that it is not at the base of the gingival sulcus (1 mm)
    3. An allowance for the biologic width of the gingival attachment (about 2 mm)
  • Thus, if a fracture is at the height of the alveolar crest, the tooth should be extruded about 3 mm; if it is 2 mm below the crest, 5 mm of extrusion ideally would be needed.
  • The crown-to-root ratio at the end of treatment should be 1:1 or better. A tooth with a poorer ratio can be maintained only by splinting it to adjacent teeth.
  • In general, extrusion can be as rapid as 1 mm per week without damage to the PDL.
Reframed (7th) The 7th reframes controlled extrusion as an alternative to light continuous forces combined with crown-lengthening surgery, and states the preferred method is now a heavy base wire with a light (usually NiTi) overlay wire. It also corrects the esthetics: the apparent crown length is increased (your summary, from the 6th, says "maintained"), and lists the risks as tissue damage, tooth devitalization, and ankylosis.

Orthodontic Technique for Extrusion

  • Because extrusion occurs most readily and intrusion occurs least readily, ample anchorage is usually available from adjacent teeth. Fig 19.16
  • Two methods are suggested for extrusion in uncomplicated cases:
    1. A stabilizing wire, 19 × 25 or 21 × 25 stainless steel, bonded directly to the facial surface of the adjacent teeth Fig 19.17.
    2. Bond brackets to the anchor teeth, bond an attachment (often a button rather than a bracket) to the tooth to be extruded, and use interarch elastics Fig 19.18 or a flexible archwire Fig 19.19.
  • With any technique for controlled extrusion, the patient must be seen every 1 to 2 weeks to remove any occlusal contacts that would impede eruption.
  • After active tooth movement has been completed, a period of at least 3 weeks but not more than 6 weeks of stabilization is needed to allow reorganization of the PDL. (Why not 3 months?)

IV Alignment of Anterior Teeth

Diastema Closure and Space Redistribution

  • The major indication for adjunctive orthodontic treatment to correct malaligned anterior teeth is preparation for buildups, veneers, or implants to improve the appearance of the maxillary incisor teeth.
  • A "diagnostic set-up" is very helpful in planning the correction of such problems.
  • There are two possible orthodontic techniques: a partial fixed appliance, typically with bonded brackets on most if not all the maxillary teeth and a bonded tube on the first molars for additional anchorage control, or a sequence of clear aligners.

Crowded, Rotated, and Displaced Incisors

  • Whether the crowding should be resolved by expanding the arch, IPR, or removing one lower incisor.
  • Expansion and IPR: can provide space for alignment of mildly irregular lower incisors, and either a fixed appliance or a clear aligner sequence can provide the tooth movement.
  • In severe crowding, removing one lower incisor and using the space to align the other three incisors can produce a satisfactory result and can be managed with clear aligner therapy.
  • Neither stripping nor incisor extraction should be undertaken without a diagnostic set-up to verify feasibility.
New section — OSA & orthodontics (7th) The 7th adds a section on obstructive sleep apnea here:
  • Mandibular-advancement oral appliances completely resolve OSA in only 29% to 71% of patients (~⅓ get no therapeutic effect). The concept of "mean disease alleviation" explains why appliances (less effective but worn more) and CPAP (very effective but used less) can give equivalent cardiovascular/quality-of-life outcomes, even in severe OSA.
  • Dental side effects: at 10+ years, advancement appliances reduce overjet and overbite by 2 to 3 mm (progressive with each year), often forming anterior crossbites.
  • CPAP (nasal-mask type) can cause anterior dental spacing from proclination — so these patients should also be given orthodontic retainers. Stopping OSA treatment should only be done under a physician's direction, with alternative therapy (e.g., CPAP) in place.
Comprehensive Treatment in Adults

I Psychologic Considerations

  • A patient with internal motivation is more likely to respond well psychologically than externally motivated.
  • Patients with an inadequate or pathologic personality Fig 19.23 are more likely to have a complex set of unrecognized expectations for treatment.
  • If patient thinks that appearance or function of the teeth is creating a severe problem but an assessment simply does not corroborate that, orthodontic treatment should be approached with caution.
  • Adults, as a rule, are less tolerant of discomfort and more likely to complain about pain after adjustments and about difficulties in speech, eating, and tissue adaptation.

II Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment

Types of Problems

  • TMD patients are classified in four large groups: masticatory muscle disorders, TM joint disorders, chronic mandibular hypomobility, or growth disorders. Fig 19.24
  • Because muscle spasm and joint pathology can coexist, the distinction in many patients is difficult.
  • Men with severe malocclusion, occlusal characteristics are directly associated with health-related quality.
  • Displacement of the disc is increasingly frequent as age increases and can arise from a number of causes. One possibility is trauma to the joint such that the ligaments that oppose the action of the lateral pterygoid muscle are stretched or torn. (the ligaments do not restore the disk to its proper position when the jaw is closed). The result is a click on opening and closing.
  • The click and symptoms associated with it can be corrected if an occlusal splint is used to prevent the patient from closing the jaw beyond the point at which displacement occurs. The resulting relief of pain influences patients and dentists to seek either restorative or orthodontic treatment to increase facial vertical dimension. (not a treatment procedure that should be undertaken lightly) (Usually there are better ways of handling disc displacement than orthodontic treatment)
  • To produce myofascial pain, the patient must be clenching or grinding the teeth for many hours per day, presumably as a response to stress. It is impossible to say that occlusal discrepancies of any given degree will lead to TMD symptoms, although recent multicenter research has at least clarified the possibilities.
  • It is possible to demonstrate that some types of occlusal discrepancies predispose patients who clench or grind their teeth to the development of TMD symptoms. It must be kept in mind, however, that it takes two factors to produce myofascial pain: an occlusal discrepancy and a patient who clenches or grinds the teeth.

Treatment Indications

  • Three broad approaches to myofascial pain symptoms can be considered: reducing the amount of stress; reducing the patients' reactions to stress; or improving the occlusion.
  • Drastic alteration of the occlusion, by either restorative dental procedures or orthodontics, is logical only if the less invasive stress-control and stress-adaptation approaches have failed. (this may involve orthognathic surgery to reposition the jaws)
  • Orthodontic intervention can appear almost magical in the way that TMD symptoms disappear long before the occlusal relationships have been corrected. (grinding or clenching sensitive teeth might break the habit)
  • The changing occlusal relationships also contribute to breaking up the habit patterns that contributed to the muscle fatigue and pain.
  • Prolonged use of Class II or Class III elastics may not be well tolerated in adults who have had TMD problems and should be avoided (prolonged use of elastics should be avoided in most other adult patients as well).
  • Sometimes, the clenching and grinding that originally caused the problem tend to recur after the orthodontic treatment is completed, the use of interocclusal splints in this situation may be the only way to keep symptoms from recurring.
  • Occasionally, orthodontic treatment is made more complicated by previous splint therapy. "open the bite posteriorly" Fig 19.27 (Placing orthodontic attachments on the posterior teeth and using light vertical elastics can be used to bring the posterior teeth back into occlusion)

III Periodontal Considerations

  • The prevalence of periodontal disease as a function of age in a large group of potential orthodontic patients with severe malocclusion is shown in Fig 19.29.
  • The odds are that any patient over the age of 35 has some periodontal problems that could affect orthodontic treatment, and mucogingival considerations are important in treatment of the younger adult group.
  • The best indicator that disease may be present is a history of disease. At present, persistent bleeding on gentle probing is the best indicator of active and presumably progressive disease.

Treatment of Patients With Minimal Periodontal Involvement (10% of the periodontal patients)

  • In children and adolescents, even if gingivitis develops in response to the presence of orthodontic appliances, it almost never extends into periodontitis. This cannot be taken for granted in adults.
  • Two characteristics are important regarding recession: the width of the attached gingiva (not all keratinized gingiva is attached) and the thickness of the gingival tissue.
  • Lingually tipped lower incisors in patients with a prominent chin have a high risk of recession, and thin gingival tissue probably is the reason
  • Gingival graft (before orthodontic treatment) must be considered in adults with minimal attached gingiva or thin tissue, particularly those for whom arch expansion will be used to align incisors and those who will have surgical mandibular advancement or genioplasty (because surgical incisions stretch the gingiva as they heal)

Moderate Periodontal Involvement (80% of the periodontal patients)

  • Treatment procedures to facilitate the patient's long-term maintenance, such as osseous recontouring or repositioned flaps to compensate for areas of gingival recession, are best deferred until the final occlusal relationships have been established.
  • The general guideline for preliminary restorative treatment is that temporary restorations should be placed to control caries, with the definitive restorative dentistry delayed until after the orthodontic phase. (Composite resin is now the preferred temporary restorative material while orthodontics is being carried out. Cast restorations should be delayed until after the final occlusal relationships have been established)
  • For more plaque control in periodontally involved adults:
    • Use a fully bonded orthodontic appliance (rather than of bands)
    • Use self-ligating brackets or steel ligatures (rather than elastomeric rings)
  • During comprehensive orthodontics, a patient with moderate periodontal problems must be on a maintenance schedule (2 to 4 month intervals is the usual plan).

Severe Periodontal Involvement (10% of the periodontal patients)

  • Orthodontic treatment can be carried out without further loss of alveolar bone if good control of the periodontal condition is maintained.
  • The treatment itself must be modified in two ways:
    • Periodontal maintenance should be scheduled at more frequent intervals (every 4 to 6 weeks)
    • Orthodontic treatment goals and mechanics must be modified to keep orthodontic forces to an absolute minimum Fig 19.32
  • The crown‒root ratio is a significant factor in the long-term prognosis for a tooth that has sustained periodontal bone loss.
  • In adults with bone loss and an anterior deep bite, the orthodontist should not hesitate to remove part of the crown of elongated lower incisors as an alternative to intrusion (simplify orthodontic leveling of the arch and improve the periodontal prognosis).
  • Space closure in areas of major bone loss sometimes leads to an improvement in bone height if at least one wall of the periodontal pocket remains.

IV Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions

Problems Related to Loss of Tooth Structure

  • The ideal buccolingual position of a worn or damaged maxillary tooth would be influenced by how the restoration was planned. If crowns are planned, the tooth should be in the center of the dental arch without tight contact with the opposing arch. But if a facial veneer is to be used for an incisor or canine the orthodontist should place the tooth more lingually, in contact with its antagonist in the lower arch.
  • Better restorations can be done if the orthodontist provides slightly more space than is required, so there is room for the restorative dentist to finish and polish proximal surfaces. The slight excess space can then be closed with a retainer.
  • If only a small amount of tooth structure has been lost (fractured incisal edge)‒it may be possible to elongate the damaged tooth so that the incisal edges line up. The result, however, will be uneven gingival margins. More than 1 to 2 mm of elongation rarely is a good plan unless patient never exposes the gingiva.

Gingival Esthetic Problems

  • Two categories: excessive/uneven display of gingiva, and gingival recession after periodontal bone loss.
  • Substituting a canine on one side will result in uneven gingival margins unless great care is taken to extrude the canine and reduce its crown height.
  • The best approach to "black triangles" problem is to remove some interproximal enamel so that the incisors can be brought closer together.

Missing Teeth: Space Closure Versus Prosthetic Replacement

Old Extraction Sites

  • If there is buccolingual narrowing of the alveolar process in the extraction site, closing the extraction space requires a reshaping of the cortical bone that comprises the buccal and lingual plates of the alveolar process. Cortical bone will respond to orthodontic force in most instances, but the response is significantly slower. Uprighting (~6 months) Vs Space closure (~3 years)
  • Often, it is better judgment to open a partially closed old extraction site and replace the missing tooth.

Tooth Loss Due to Periodontal Disease

  • Sometimes, closure of the space where a hopelessly involved tooth was extracted results in an improvement of the periodontal situation. Unless at least one bony wall remains, however, it is better to move teeth away from such an area in preparation for a prosthetic replacement, because normal bone formation cannot be expected as the tooth moves into the defect.
  • However, there is an exception. First molars and incisors are lost in some adolescents and young adults to aggressive juvenile periodontitis (due to Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans). It often is possible to orthodontically close the extraction sites, bringing the second permanent molar forward. The second molar brings its own investing bone with it, and the large bony defect disappears. This favorable response is attributed to some combination of three factors: the relatively young patients, the fact that the original attack was almost entirely on the first molars, and the change in the bacterial flora.
  • In an older patient who lost a first molar to periodontal disease, it is unlikely that the other teeth have been totally spared or that the bacterial flora have changed, and it would not be good judgment to attempt to close the space.

Comprehensive Orthodontics in Patients in Whom Implants Are Planned

  • The patient should be ready for definitive prosthodontic treatment as soon as possible after the orthodontic appliances are removed (place bone grafts in areas that will receive implants while orthodontic treatment is being carried out) (osseointegration during the orthodontic treatment is advantageous)
  • Almost always, a fixed orthodontic retainer is the best choice to maintain a space for an implant.
  • In the anterior area, patients often prefer a temporary resin-bonded bridge.
  • A damaged and ankylosed maxillary incisor or canine in a teenager poses a special problem, alveolar atrophy will occur if the tooth is extracted before vertical growth is completed and the implant can be placed. In this situation, the alveolar bone can be "banked" by removing the crown of the offending tooth but retaining the endodontically treated root, or simply decoronating the tooth without endodontic treatment.
  • An implant too soon creates a major problem. The implant becomes the equivalent of an ankylosed tooth and will appear to intrude as vertical development continues and the other teeth erupt Fig 19.39.

V Complex Treatment Procedures

Lingual Orthodontics

  • The most advanced current lingual technique uses a custom-formed pad for each tooth to provide more secure bonding of the appliance, and computer-controlled wire-bending robots to generate the archwires.
  • In lingual orthodontics, the wire-bending robots are an important part of the system. They provide compensation for an unavoidable problem, "the short distances between the teeth on the lingual aspect".
  • It can be hard to align severely crowded lower incisors without reshaping the archwires, including the A-NiTi wire for initial alignment.
  • With lingually bonded brackets and archwires, any type of tooth movement now can be produced quite efficiently,

Clear Aligner Therapy in Complex Cases

  • Treating complex cases with Invisalign or its clear aligner competitors is deceptively similar to treatment of less severe problems, but there are three big differences:
    1. The sequence of steps typically used by the computer system technicians typically needs to be modified
    2. The direction and amount of movement of teeth produced by the standard algorithms often are reduced
    3. New records and a new set of revision aligners often are needed during the treatment process. (it is better to set an initial goal that is an intermediate to the final goal and then establish the sequence of aligners starting from there to complete the treatment. "the golf analogy")
De-branded & relocated (7th) The 7th drops the brand names and the "almost prohibitively expensive / compliance" caveat, deferring detail to the new adult-aligner chapter: "clear tray treatment for adults is described in Chapter 21" (tray production in Chapter 10).

Applications of Skeletal Anchorage

Retraction of Protruding Incisors

  • Maxilla: An implant in the center of the palate can be used to stabilize a lingual arch that prevents movement of the molars to which it is attached, but stabilization away from the midline is better and both direct and indirect anchorage are available as desired Fig 19.44.
  • Mandible: Can be managed best with alveolar bone screws in the buccal shelf below the molars.
  • In Asian adults who had significant retraction of incisors to correct bimaxillary protrusion, bony spicules sometimes appear between the roots of the teeth Fig 19.46A, they are created by differential remodeling of alveolar bone as the teeth are moved posteriorly (NOT bony exostoses)

Retraction and Intrusion of Protruding Incisors

  • With segmented arch mechanics, maxillary incisors can be both retracted and intruded if excellent anchorage is maintained with stabilizing lingual arches and headgear if necessary.
  • If retraction and intrusion are needed, skeletal anchorage now is recommended. With alveolar bone screws between the molar roots or miniplates at the base of the zygomatic arch, the direction of force, both upward and backward, is ideal for this purpose, and A-NiTi retraction springs provide a constant known force level.

Distal Movement of Molars or the Entire Dental Arch

  • Maxillary Distalization: Miniplates below the zygomatic arch or palatal bone screws provide a predictable outcome. Bone screws in the alveolar process interfere with root movement and are not recommended. Single bone screws in the infrazygomatic process away from the roots are a possibility but may not withstand the amount of force needed to move multiple teeth. The entire arch usually can be moved back 2 to 4 mm. More than that usually requires extraction of the second molars.
  • Mandibular Distalization: a long bone screw into the mandibular buccal shelf or ramus
  • Molar Protraction: indirect anchorage to stabilize the anterior dental segments, from bone screws in the palate for maxillary molar protraction and in the mandibular buccal shelf or ramus for the mandible Figs 19.47, 19.48.

Intrusion

  • Intrusion of incisors: In adolescents and young adults with excessive overbite, the choice between intrusion of incisors or extrusion of posterior teeth often can be resolved in favor of extrusion (vertical growth will compensate). In adults, the choice often must be intrusion, which is more effective when skeletal anchorage in the form of miniplates or screws is available and when segmented rather than continuous archwires are used.
  • With intrusion in adults with periodontal involvement, what happen is the formation of a tight epithelial cuff, so that the position of the gingiva relative to the crown improves clinically while periodontal probing depths do not increase.
  • Intrusion of Posterior Teeth to Close Anterior Open Bite: Skeletal anchorage to intrude the posterior teeth has the potential to create the same mandibular response Fig 19.50. For intrusion of maxillary posterior teeth, miniplates at the base of the zygomatic arch provide excellent anchorage. The fixture for attachment to the orthodontic appliance extends through the soft tissue, preferably at the junction between gingiva and mucosa. A long bone screw extending into the base of the zygomatic arch, which orthodontists with experience with alveolar bone screws can place, is a possible alternative. (through attached gingiva)
  • Some preliminary separation of roots in the region in which the screw will be placed makes it easier to avoid root contact and is recommended Fig 19.51.
  • An ideal force system for intrusion is created by A-NiTi springs (constant known force over a considerable range of activation).
  • An upward force on the facial aspect of the posterior teeth is also a force to tip them facially, and control to prevent this is essential. Transpalatal lingual arches are one possibility, but controlling all the teeth in the segment being intruded is necessary. A bonded plate (modified Erverdi appliance) covering the occlusal surface of the teeth, fabricated so that it is off the palate enough to allow the intrusion, is the preferred method at present.
  • It may be advantageous to have a Class II or Class III component to the force so that the maxillary arch is moved a little forward or back as the intrusion occurs Fig 19.52.
  • Even with appropriate light force (not more than 200 gm to a three-tooth posterior segment), intrusion does not occur as quickly as other types of tooth movement. Space closure and most other types of movement occur at the rate of about 1 mm per month. At best, posterior intrusion occurs at half that rate.
  • Because 1 mm intrusion of maxillary posterior teeth should translate into about 2 mm of closure of anterior open bite, a 4-mm open bite often closes in as many months.
  • Box 19.2 shows that eruption of lower molars was a major factor in achieving less mandibular rotation than was expected during active intrusion. Lower molar eruption during maxillary molar intrusion was the major reason for failure to obtain the expected change in anterior dimensions, and further eruption during the orthodontic treatment continued to be a factor in relapse.
  • In summary:
    • Maxillary molar intrusion can give satisfactory correction of moderately severe open bite (up to 6 mm in the long term from intrusion, more with extrusion of incisors).
    • Control of lower molar eruption now is recognized as important in gaining the desired skeletal change and should be included routinely when maxillary molar intrusion is done.
    • Clinical experience suggests that intrusion of both maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth can allow closure of more severe open bites (more than 6 mm open bite)
    • Eruption of maxillary and/or mandibular incisors partially compensates for re-rotation of the mandible (after treatment), so bite opening after open bite correction (by posterior teeth intrusion) rarely occurs.
